chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
title: McShann underrated; Earl Hines the same
summary: McShann is introduced only as Parker's discoverer, and Hines too is asked mainly about others.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well, I've sort of begun to think about him, is that he's easy-going, or he's a pleasant sort of personality. As a result of this the man has been frankly underrated.

Yeah. We were talking about that, too. It kind of hurts him, but he doesn't let that show, you know. He mentioned one time, he said that, "everybody's introducing me as the man who just up and discovered Charlie Parker."
And not so much for his own ability, what he contributed, you know.
He mentioned it a couple times. He said, you know, someday they'll all recognize me, you know.
Well, you know, it's exactly the same

with Earl Hines. When he was in New York this last time, I said, for God's sake, let me sit in on these interviews, because the people come in, and they make him mad because all they want to talk about really is Louis Armstrong and Charlie Parker. And, you know, the fact of the matter is, if you don't seem to realize that this man, for 20 years, led one of the best big bands in the country --
And had everybody trying to play like him.
And it was an innovator. I mean, I don't blame him -- you know, that gets him annoyed.
